article_title: Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs
citation: Youssef Medhat, Junsoo Park, Ploy Thajchayapong and Ashok K. Goel. (2026). Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs. CSEDM'26: 10th Workshop on Computer Science Educational Data Mining. https://dilab.gatech.edu
title: GPT-4-extracted curriculum prerequisite knowledge graph (54 topic nodes, 47 directed prerequisite edges)
description: A prerequisite knowledge graph extracted by GPT-4 from 26 lesson PDFs of a graduate-level AI course, following a three-stage protocol of topic extraction, boundary consolidation, and edge extraction. The graph contains "54 topic nodes and 47 directed prerequisite edges" and serves two roles: its topic nodes provide the closed label space for classification and survey alignment, and its directed prerequisite edges encode curriculum structure for future per-student gap propagation. The authors describe it as "a low-cost, instructor-auditable way to obtain a topic–edge artifact".
requirements: A course instructor with domain expertise to run and audit the GPT-4 extraction protocol over lesson PDFs
constraints: The authors do not claim the graph is the unique correct structure; only unambiguous, non-bidirectional GPT-4 prerequisite judgments are retained
target_learners: graduate-level AI course students
target_learning_goals: mapping student questions to curriculum topics
identifying topic-level knowledge gaps
examples: Sample extracted edges include Semantic Networks → Frames, Case-Based Reasoning → Analogical Reasoning, and Logic → Explanation-Based Learning, matching the course textbook's lesson ordering
key_sources: Youssef Medhat, Junsoo Park, Ploy Thajchayapong and Ashok K. Goel. (2026). Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs. CSEDM'26: 10th Workshop on Computer Science Educational Data Mining. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10736

article_title: When Youth Enter The Chat: An Epistemic Shift in the Validation of LLM-Based Measures of Student Talk
citation: Liliana Santos-Deonizio, James Malamut, Ramón Antonio Martínez, and Dorottya Demszky. (2027). When Youth Enter The Chat: An Epistemic Shift in the Validation of LLM-Based Measures of Student Talk. In Proceedings of TBD (CSCW '27). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23780
title: LLM-based talk-move annotation pipeline using GPT-5.1 with a multi-theoretic codebook
description: The article describes an LLM-based measurement pipeline in which classroom recordings are transcribed by automated speech recognition with human cleanup, then annotated by GPT-5.1. "We used GPT-5.1 to annotate the transcripts chosen for the student member checks." The model was prompted with code definitions and three positive examples and three non-examples per code, assigning each sentence-level utterance binary labels for topic codes (Off-task, Recording, Competent, Understanding, Tool) and talk-move codes (Question, Apology, Claim, Reasoning, Next Step, Monitor, Disagree, Agree, Compare, Add-On, Revoice).
requirements: A human-expert-annotated validation set
Code definitions developed with human experts
Prompting with code definitions and worked examples per code
constraints: The article reports low F1 for some features, most notably Next-Step and Disagree, even after definition updates
target_learners: middle school math students in multilingual classrooms
target_learning_goals: measuring collaborative and academic talk moves in student discourse
examples: GPT-5.1 was selected over Claude 3.7 and GPT 5.0 based on F1 scores against the validation set
key_sources: Liliana Santos-Deonizio, James Malamut, Ramón Antonio Martínez, and Dorottya Demszky. (2027). When Youth Enter The Chat: An Epistemic Shift in the Validation of LLM-Based Measures of Student Talk. In Proceedings of TBD (CSCW '27). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23780

article_title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
citation: Bastani Hamsa, Bastani Osbert, Sungu Alp, Ge Haosen, Kabakcı Özge, Mariman Rei. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122
title: GPT Tutor: a guardrailed GPT-4 math tutor that gives teacher-designed hints instead of answers
description: GPT Tutor is a GPT-4 chat interface whose system prompt implements safeguards: it is instructed to "provide hints to the student without directly giving them the answer, to encourage learning", and it receives problem-specific teacher inputs including correct solutions, common student mistakes, and feedback guidance. This prevents hallucinated answers and makes the tool hard to use as a crutch. Students do not see the system prompts.
requirements: Problem-specific teacher inputs (solutions, common mistakes, hints) must be prepared for each practice problem, which the article notes is labor-intensive.
constraints: The article notes GPT Tutor remains passive, responding to questions rather than proactively engaging students with the material.
target_learners: High school mathematics students (grades 9-11)
target_learning_goals: Review and mastery of previously covered mathematics topics
examples: Deployed in four 90-minute sessions across about fifty 9th-11th grade classes in a Turkish high school, with students solving teacher-designed practice problems.
key_sources: Bastani Hamsa, Bastani Osbert, Sungu Alp, Ge Haosen, Kabakcı Özge, Mariman Rei. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122

article_title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
citation: Escalante, J., Pack, A., & Barrett, A. (2023). AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:57. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00425-2
title: Role-based GPT-4 prompt for six-area corrective writing feedback
description: A structured prompt, developed iteratively by two experienced language educators, that casts GPT-4 as "a professional language teacher who is an expert on providing feedback on the writing of English language learners". It instructs the model, using simple language, to comment on six areas: topic sentence, development of ideas, language lowering academic quality, transitional phrases, use of sources and evidence, and grammatical accuracy, with grammar feedback organized into a four-column error table (sentence, error type, description, suggestion). A teaching assistant ran the prompt per student and emailed feedback within two working days.
requirements: Prompt engineering following the framework of Ingley and Pack (2023); de-identified student drafts; GPT-4 access
constraints: GPT-4 is not optimized for AWE purposes, so features like text annotation common in existing AWE programs are cumbersome to reproduce
target_learners: ENL university students writing 300-word academic paragraphs
target_learning_goals: Formative corrective feedback on academic paragraph writing
examples: Appendix B prints the full sample prompt; Appendix C shows example feedback on a student paragraph about culture, including a grammar error table
key_sources: Escalante, J., Pack, A., & Barrett, A. (2023). AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:57. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00425-2

article_title: Chatting and cheating: Ensuring academic integrity in the era of ChatGPT
citation: Debby R. E. Cotton, Peter A. Cotton & J. Reuben Shipway (2024) Chatting and cheating: Ensuring academic integrity in the era of ChatGPT, Innovations in Education and Teaching International, 61:2, 228-239. https://doi.org/10.1080/14703297.2023.2190148
title: GPT-2 Output Detector Demo as an AI-text identification tool
description: The GPT-2 Output Detector Demo is a language-analysis tool the article names as designed to analyse the language of written work and identify patterns or irregularities indicating chatbot authorship. In the authors' December 2022 trial, ten genuine student essays scored under 1% fake probability while ChatGPT essays on the same subjects scored close to 100%, and prompting changes only lowered this to around 97%.
requirements: Submitted text to analyse; works best, per the article's trial, on unmodified ChatGPT output
constraints: The article frames detection as an arms race and notes ChatGPT's ongoing training may erode detector advantage; prompting to emulate student writing only reduced scores to around 97%
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: detecting AI-generated submissions
academic integrity
examples: The authors submitted ten student essays in December 2022 and matching ChatGPT-generated essays to the detector
key_sources: Debby R. E. Cotton, Peter A. Cotton & J. Reuben Shipway (2024) Chatting and cheating: Ensuring academic integrity in the era of ChatGPT, Innovations in Education and Teaching International, 61:2, 228-239. https://doi.org/10.1080/14703297.2023.2190148

article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition
citation: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6
title: GPT-4o-generated personalized explanatory feedback for open-ended practice
description: In Study 2, the explanatory feedback condition used GPT-4o to "provide immediate, tailored explanatory feedback after each practice item", evaluating open-ended responses in real time. The prompt instructed the model to state "Correct!" or "Incorrect", explain why incorrect answers were wrong, and edit the student's exact wording with the smallest possible changes into a corrected version. Manual review of all 309 AI-generated responses found the AI correctly scored 90% of correct answers and 98% of incorrect answers, with appropriate corrections 98% of the time and no hallucinations.
requirements: GPT-4o must be given a written explanation of the problem, the criteria expected in a correct answer, and sample correct and incorrect responses based on pilot work to ensure feedback accuracy.
constraints: Accuracy was validated for this study's three regression questions and judged "sufficiently accurate for our research purposes", not as a general-purpose tutoring guarantee.
target_learners: Adult online learners practicing open-ended statistics questions
target_learning_goals: Interpreting slope and intercept of a regression line
Generating correct open-ended explanations of statistical concepts
examples: For a student who wrote only that the intercept intersects the Y axis at 5.58, the AI identified the missing interpretation and supplied a corrected version stating the predicted murder rate when temperature equals zero.
key_sources: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6

article_title: Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236
title: Game Performance Assessment Instrument (GPAI) as the most utilized in-game performance tool in PE
description: The GPAI is an observational tool developed and validated in 1998 specifically for PE settings, used to assess in-game performance variables such as skill execution and tactical variables (e.g., decision-making with the ball and off-ball support), with observations coded as successful/effective or unsuccessful/ineffective, typically during a game or from postgame video. The review reports that "the GPAI has become the most utilized tool to assess in-game performance (e.g., skill execution and tactical variables) in PE and sport school settings". Related tools named are the Team Sport Assessment Procedure (TSAP) and Game Performance Evaluation Tool (GPET).
requirements: Observation during a game or postgame recording, often via video
Trained coding of observed behaviours as successful or unsuccessful
constraints: The review notes some studies used modified versions without reporting reliability or validation, or used tools in settings different from those they were validated in
target_learners: Primary and secondary school physical education students
target_learning_goals: Assessing in-game skill execution and tactical decision-making
examples: Included studies applied the GPAI in small-sided games such as 3v3, 4v4, and 5v5 formats with postgame video
key_sources: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236

article_title: Supplemental Material for The Dynamic Interplay Between Goal Setting, Performance, and Emotions in Self-Regulated Learning: A Computational Modeling Approach
citation: The Dynamic Interplay Between Goal Setting, Performance, and Emotions in Self-Regulated Learning: A Computational Modeling Approach — Supplementary Materials. (2022). https://gpemodel.shinyapps.io/gpe-model/
title: A dynamic computational model of goal setting, performance, and emotions in self-regulated learning
description: The article presents a three-equation dynamic model in which goals, performance, and emotions at each time point are each computed as a baseline intercept, an autoregressive carry-over component, a goal-performance discrepancy (GPD) component, an emotions component (for goals and performance), and random error. The model relies on tasks where participants specify goals, complete a task, and report emotion valence across repeated goal-striving episodes. It is estimated hierarchically in Stan with 95% HDIs used for significance.
requirements: Tasks must allow participants to specify goals, obtain performance, and indicate the valence of their state emotions at each time point
Estimation requires a hierarchical Bayesian framework with MCMC sampling and 95% HDIs for parameter significance
constraints: The first block is not predicted because there are no prior goal levels, performances, and emotions
No constraints on the values that goal levels, performances, and emotions could take were set
target_learners: adult participants in achievement tasks
self-regulated learners
target_learning_goals: goal setting
performance self-regulation
emotional responses to goal striving
examples: Applied to an online math task in Study 1 and to multi-day self-regulated studying in Study 2
key_sources: The Dynamic Interplay Between Goal Setting, Performance, and Emotions in Self-Regulated Learning: A Computational Modeling Approach — Supplementary Materials. (2022). https://gpemodel.shinyapps.io/gpe-model/

article_title: Supplemental Material for The Dynamic Interplay Between Goal Setting, Performance, and Emotions in Self-Regulated Learning: A Computational Modeling Approach
citation: The Dynamic Interplay Between Goal Setting, Performance, and Emotions in Self-Regulated Learning: A Computational Modeling Approach — Supplementary Materials. (2022). https://gpemodel.shinyapps.io/gpe-model/
title: Shiny App for simulating and visualizing the goals-performance-emotions model
description: The article released a Shiny App, coded in R, that lets users simulate data from the hypothesized model and visualize how different parameter values change the dynamics of goals, performance, and emotions. The authors used it to choose population-level parameter values for the parameter recovery simulation, and it is publicly accessible at the printed URL. It serves as a demonstration and simulation tool accompanying the computational model.
requirements: Users need information on how to simulate data, which the article says is provided alongside the app
target_learners: researchers studying self-regulated learning
target_learning_goals: understanding dynamics of goals, performance, and emotions
examples: Used to draw individual parameter values for 300 fictitious participants in the parameter recovery simulation

article_title: Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement
citation: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9
title: GPAΔ: a continuous genomically predicted achievement discrepancy index (observed achievement minus GPS)
description: GPAΔ (Genomically-Predicted Achievement Discrepancy) is a continuous difference score created by subtracting a standardized genome-wide polygenic score (EA4, based on educational attainment) from standardized observed achievement. The authors state they "devised an index called Genomically-Predicted Achievement Discrepancy (GPAΔ) by subtracting a GPS for adult educational attainment from educational achievement at age 7." Negative scores indicate underachievement and positive scores overachievement, spanning a continuum rather than dichotomizing students. Domain-specific versions (English–GPS, Mathematics–GPS) were also constructed.
requirements: Requires genotyping and creation of a genome-wide polygenic score, plus assessed early school achievement to compute the difference
constraints: Until a GWA study is done on GPAΔ per se, GPAΔ requires that early school achievement is assessed so the difference between GPS and observed achievement can be obtained
GPS predictive power is attenuated in populations with different ancestries; the study included only participants of European ancestry
target_learners: children in the early school years (age 7)
target_learning_goals: identifying academic underachievement and overachievement for personalized educational support
examples: In the TEDS cohort, GPAΔ at age 7 was computed for 4175 genotyped participants and correlated with achievement slopes across ages 7, 9, 12, and 16
key_sources: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9

article_title: Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement
citation: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9
title: Use genomic discrepancy indices as an early-warning system to target underachievers early, pending intervention tests
description: The article proposes GPAΔ screening as an early-warning system: because GPS are stable from conception, they can flag likely underachievers before achievement falls far behind, when interventions are most likely to succeed. The authors argue "Targeting GPAΔ underachievers might prove cost-effective because such interventions seem more likely to succeed by going with the genetic ﬂow rather than swimming upstream." This remains an explicitly untested hypothesis requiring intervention research.
requirements: Intervention research testing whether GPAΔ underachievers respond better to intervention than other underachievers
Early school achievement must be assessed to compute the GPS–achievement difference
constraints: Interventions effective for GPAΔ underachievers might be less effective in preventing the decline of GPAΔ overachievers
GPAΔ currently requires DNA, genotyping, and GPS creation; predictive power represents an upper bound for European-ancestry samples
target_learners: children in the early school years, particularly those underachieving relative to genomic prediction
target_learning_goals: early identification of underachievement to personalize education and maximize achievement toward individual potential
examples: The study screened 4175 TEDS participants at age 7 and charted trajectories showing underachievers regressing about one-third toward genomic prediction by age 16
key_sources: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9

article_title: How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses
citation: Jionghao Lin, Zifei Han, Danielle R. Thomas, Ashish Gurung, Shivang Gupta, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2024). How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00970
title: GPT-4-based explanatory feedback system for tutor training
description: An automated feedback system built on the GPT-4 model that identifies trainees' responses in binary form (correct/incorrect) and provides template-based feedback with incorrect responses rephrased by GPT-4. The system targets novice tutors in scenario-based training lessons on an online learning platform. As the authors state, "our study employed the GPT-4 model to build an explanatory feedback system", integrating the classifier and rephrasing results into real-time feedback during training sessions.
requirements: Requires a binary classifier (the 5-shot GPT-4 classifier) to pinpoint incorrect responses before rephrasing
Requires lesson-specific principles and scenario text as prompt inputs
constraints: Evaluated only on three lessons; the authors call for broader evaluation on other lessons
Binary correct/incorrect classification may be overly simplistic for real-world applications, per the authors
target_learners: novice tutors (trainees), including community volunteers, retired individuals, and college students
target_learning_goals: effective praise
reacting to student errors
determining what students know
examples: The system presents template-based suggestions such as "AI-generated feedback suggests that your response could focus more on praising the student for their efforts in the learning process."
key_sources: Jionghao Lin, Zifei Han, Danielle R. Thomas, Ashish Gurung, Shivang Gupta, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2024). How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00970

article_title: Creating Terminological Correspondence Recognition Tests with GPT-4: A Case Study in English-to-Turkish Translations in the Engineering Domain
citation: Marina Sánchez-Torrón, Egemen Ipek, Vanessa Enríquez Raído. (2024). Creating subject competence translation tests with GPT-4: A case study in English-to-Turkish translations in the engineering domain. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4187415/v1
title: GPT-4-generated English-to-Turkish subject competence MCQ tests
description: An artifact of five automatically generated multiple-choice subject competence tests for assessing translators' knowledge of engineering terminology in English-to-Turkish translation. "We generated ve subject-area assessment tests, each composed of 20 questions." Each question presents an English sentence containing an engineering term and four Turkish answer options, generated via a zero-shot prompt in OpenAI Playground with specified sampling settings. The tests were evaluated by one expert translator but, per the authors, "are not t for direct implementation without further rement".
requirements: Requires detailed prompts specifying format, cognate avoidance, distractor similarity, and CSV output
constraints: Not fit for direct implementation without further refinement
Proprietary GPT-4 makes results non-reproducible
Findings may vary across domains and language pairs
target_learners: Professional translators and post-editors in human-in-the-loop translation workflows
target_learning_goals: Subject (domain-specific) competence in engineering terminology for post-editing machine translation output
examples: Five tests of 20 questions each were generated in July 2023 via an iterative zero-shot prompt refined over 18 iterations and about 6 hours
key_sources: Marina Sánchez-Torrón, Egemen Ipek, Vanessa Enríquez Raído. (2024). Creating subject competence translation tests with GPT-4: A case study in English-to-Turkish translations in the engineering domain. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4187415/v1

article_title: Science Instruction through the Game and Physical Activities Course: An Interdisciplinary Teaching Practice
citation: Celal Boyraz, Gökhan Serin. (2017). Science Instruction through the Game and Physical Activities Course: An Interdisciplinary Teaching Practice. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051119
title: Game-based physical activity plans integrating science outcomes from simple to complex across a five-week unit
description: A lesson-level design in which the outcomes of a science unit are mapped onto a sequence of game-based physical activities, integrated "from simple to complex" across five weeks. Twelve games (traditional, curriculum-based, and researcher-designed or adapted) each carried one or more science outcomes, and separate lesson plans were prepared for each timing strategy, yielding 36 plans in total. Safety outcome 4 was embedded in every plan because of the risk inherent in physical play.
requirements: Games whose rules are easily comprehended by students and that include an emphasis of competition, per the pilot study feedback
A suitable physical setting such as a school garden with game materials
constraints: Generalizability stated to hold only if the physical conditions (school garden with hoop, lines, materials) are met
Students resisted returning indoors after outdoor play, so concept discussion was built into the outdoor lesson
target_learners: elementary school third-grade students (about nine years old)
target_learning_goals: science concepts of the unit Let's Learn about Force (motion, push and pull forces)
examples: Twelve games such as Stop, Tug of War, and Flying Saucer were implemented one per lesson in the first four weeks; in week five students re-played the three activities they liked most
key_sources: Celal Boyraz, Gökhan Serin. (2017). Science Instruction through the Game and Physical Activities Course: An Interdisciplinary Teaching Practice. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051119

article_title: The impact of general pedagogical knowledge on student engagement as mediated by instructional communication.
citation: Aynalem Workineh Birhanu, Tolla Tiruwork Tamiru, Abebe Amare Sahile. (2026). The impact of general pedagogical knowledge on student engagement as mediated by instructional communication. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-60556-0
title: GPK–IC–SE conceptual framework with instructional communication as process variable
description: The article proposes a conceptual model in which general pedagogical knowledge shapes student engagement through instructional communication, "positioned as the process variable that enacts pedagogical expertise". IC refers to teachers' verbal and non-verbal behaviors characterized by clarity, immediacy, and responsiveness that shape classroom climate and interaction. The framework was tested with SEM and is presented as a theoretical model (Fig. 3) linking the three constructs.
requirements: Validated instruments measuring GPK, IC, and SE; the study adapted three instruments with five-point Likert scales
constraints: Engagement was measured exclusively through teachers' perceptions, not students' actual engagement behaviors
target_learners: College teachers in Ethiopian higher education
target_learning_goals: Instructional communication competence
Student engagement
key_sources: Aynalem Workineh Birhanu, Tolla Tiruwork Tamiru, Abebe Amare Sahile. (2026). The impact of general pedagogical knowledge on student engagement as mediated by instructional communication. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-60556-0

article_title: Implementation and evaluation of customized artificial intelligence personal tutor (chat GPT physiology companion) for medical students in the reproduction module.
citation: Elsamanoudy Ayman; Alhazimi Awdah; Hassanien Mohammed; Almarabheh Amer; Al-Aqidi Sultan; Alwalidi Raghad; Alrefaie Zienab zeinab. (2026). Implementation and evaluation of customized artificial intelligence personal tutor (chat GPT physiology companion) for medical students in the reproduction module. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09088-9
title: GPT Reproductive Physiology Companion: a customized GPT-4o AI tutoring tool for medical students
description: A customized AI companion built on the GPT-4o platform, developed using a six-step approach for customized GPTs in medical education. It was configured to align responses with the module's learning outcomes, competency framework, and national licensing examination (SMLE) blueprints. Key features included "summarized and simplified explanations of complex topics," step-by-step breakdowns of physiological pathways, mnemonic aids, clinical correlations (e.g., PCOS, infertility), audio voice-overs based on Guyton & Hall, and interactive formative assessments (MCQs and MEQs) with tiered feedback.
requirements: Access to the GPT-4o platform and an accompanying Google Drive repository for textbook materials and voice-over files
constraints: The intervention was limited to a single module and designed primarily for formative learning support rather than comprehensive exam preparation
target_learners: Third-year pre-clinical undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: Reproductive physiology conceptual understanding
Formative self-assessment
Clinical application of basic science knowledge
examples: Students accessed the tool via a dedicated chatgpt.com link during the 6-week Reproduction module for content clarification, quiz practice, clinical applications, and auditory reinforcement
key_sources: Elsamanoudy Ayman; Alhazimi Awdah; Hassanien Mohammed; Almarabheh Amer; Al-Aqidi Sultan; Alwalidi Raghad; Alrefaie Zienab zeinab. (2026). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09088-9

article_title: Endodontic diagnostics training in undergraduate dental education: An observational pilot study on AI-driven virtual patient e-learning.
citation: Prinz, M., Schäfer, E., Bürklein, S. & Donnermeyer, D. (2026) Endodontic diagnostics training in undergraduate dental education: An observational pilot study on AI‐driven virtual patient e‐learning. International Endodontic Journal, 59, 1145–1159. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.14277
title: GPT-4-turbo-based virtual patient web app for endodontic diagnostic training
description: A web-app e-learning platform with three components: a user-facing website, a MongoDB database server holding patient case information with radiographic and clinical images, and the GPT-4-turbo model (OpenAI) accessed via API. "A web app was designed to serve as the e‐learning platform consisting of three main components"; the model processes each query together with the full preceding dialogue and the complete case details. Speech recognition input and text-to-speech output enable more realistic conversation. Eight patient cases covered the most common endodontic pathologies, with diagnoses such as acute irreversible pulpitis and cracked tooth syndrome.
requirements: Precise and extensive patient case vignettes covering all diagnosis-related information and clinical tests, so the AI model can give appropriate answers
A universal system prompt with placeholders integrating case information from the database, instructing the model to answer only from the case information and to avoid hallucination
constraints: Case complexity was deliberately kept low, aligned with undergraduate students' expertise level
The model was barred from using general web information and responds "I am not sure" when case-related information is unavailable
target_learners: 4th- and 5th-year undergraduate dental students
target_learning_goals: Endodontic pain diagnostics and clinical decision-making
Patient communication and obtaining informed consent
examples: Students solved eight virtual patient cases over a 3-month individual-use period; 38.9% of participants completed all eight cases
key_sources: Prinz, M., Schäfer, E., Bürklein, S. & Donnermeyer, D. (2026) Endodontic diagnostics training in undergraduate dental education: An observational pilot study on AI‐driven virtual patient e‐learning. International Endodontic Journal, 59, 1145–1159. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.14277

article_title: Comparing AI chatbot simulation and peer role-play for OSCE preparation: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
citation: Lee Hye-Yoon, Kim Jundong, Choi Hyojae, Bae Hyojin, Jeong Aram, Choi Sungyoul, Kim Ji-Hwan, Kim Chang-Eop. (2025). Comparing AI chatbot simulation and peer role-play for OSCE preparation: a pilot randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08308-y
title: Multi-layered GPT-4o/Claude 3.5 Sonnet OSCE simulation chatbot with automated scoring and text feedback
description: A proprietary educational AI chatbot combining GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet in a multi-layered architecture, used as the experimental training tool in the pilot RCT. OSCE scenarios were "converted into chart‑style prompts optimized for SP role simulation"; the chatbot acted as a simulated patient, generated natural responses to student inquiries, and after each interview provided "both quantitative scoring and individualized text feedback based on the dialogue". Students practiced dizziness and shoulder pain cases freely without time or attempt restrictions.
requirements: Pre-designed chart-style scenario prompts; a clinical expert supervising sessions; reliable server performance and technical support on standby
constraints: Students reported inability to implement physical examination, lack of understanding of Korean medicine terminology, absence of real interaction with patients, and scoring speed delay
target_learners: final-year Korean medicine students preparing for OSCE
target_learning_goals: clinical interview and history taking
patient education
clinical reasoning
examples: In the trial, the chatbot group practiced two clinical presentations with two cases each for one hour under clinical expert supervision, submitting sessions for automated scoring and LLM-generated text feedback
key_sources: Lee Hye-Yoon, Kim Jundong, Choi Hyojae, Bae Hyojin, Jeong Aram, Choi Sungyoul, Kim Ji-Hwan, Kim Chang-Eop. (2025). Comparing AI chatbot simulation and peer role-play for OSCE preparation: a pilot randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08308-y

article_title: The effects of video-based and blended learning on medication dosage calculation skills of paramedic students: A randomized, quasi-experimental study.
citation: Baran L, Öztürk H. (2025). The effects of video-based and blended learning on medication dosage calculation skills of paramedic students: A randomized, quasi-experimental study. Medicine 104(31):e43651. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000043651
title: Use GPA-ranked systematic assignment to balance ability levels when randomizing students into instructional comparison groups
description: Because students with higher GPAs tend to achieve higher MDC test scores, the authors ranked all 158 consenting students by GPA and alternately assigned odd-ranked students to the BL group and even-ranked students to the VBL group. This systematic procedure controlled the GPA confound that simple randomization may leave unbalanced, while acknowledging that self-reported learning style and numerical competency are unreliable to stratify on.
requirements: Access to students' GPA records before assignment and a full cohort enrollment approach
constraints: Self-reported numerical competency and learning style may be inaccurate, limiting stratification on those variables
target_learners: Undergraduate health-program students participating in instructional comparison studies
target_learning_goals: Fair comparison of instructional methods on skills outcomes such as medication dosage calculation
examples: The study verified no significant GPA difference between groups (t = −1.48, P = .140) after ranked assignment
key_sources: Baran L, Öztürk H. (2025). The effects of video-based and blended learning on medication dosage calculation skills of paramedic students: A randomized, quasi-experimental study. Medicine 104(31):e43651. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000043651

article_title: Development of a GPT-4-Powered Virtual Simulated Patient and Communication Training Platform for Medical Students to Practice Discussing Abnormal Mammogram Results With Patients: Multiphase Study.
citation: Mavragani A, Chan S, Doyle AJ, Weisman D, Sugarman A, Huang YM, Gelberg L, Ganz PA, Comulada WS. (2025). Development of a GPT-4–Powered Virtual Simulated Patient and Communication Training Platform for Medical Students to Practice Discussing Abnormal Mammogram Results With Patients: Multiphase Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/65670
title: GPT-4–powered virtual simulated patient platform for practicing abnormal mammogram result conversations
description: A virtual training module built in Hyperskill (SimInsights) simulation authoring software, using automated speech recognition and text-to-speech for real-time spoken conversation with a GPT-4–driven virtual simulated patient. The final scenario flow "consisted of only 2 states (setup and feedback)", with the AI chatbot generating patient replies in real time and an AI feedback agent producing postconversation assessment with quoted examples. Medical students role-play a PCP telephoning the patient about abnormal diagnostic mammogram results requiring a biopsy.
requirements: A detailed text prompt specifying scenario context, patient emotional state, and expected responses to learner choices, iteratively refined through agile testing cycles
constraints: VSP dialogue and generated feedback are not standardized, so the authors state it is unlikely the training could currently be used in summative clinical examinations
target_learners: medical students
target_learning_goals: communicating abnormal mammogram results with patients
adhering to the SPIKES protocol for delivering difficult news
empathic patient-centered communication
examples: The scenario simulates a telephone call, depicted as a 3D cell phone on a physician's desk with a red End button that ends the conversation and triggers feedback generation.
key_sources: Mavragani A, Chan S, Doyle AJ, Weisman D, Sugarman A, Huang YM, Gelberg L, Ganz PA, Comulada WS. (2025). Development of a GPT-4–Powered Virtual Simulated Patient and Communication Training Platform for Medical Students to Practice Discussing Abnormal Mammogram Results With Patients: Multiphase Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/65670

article_title: Evaluating general practitioners' focused lung ultrasound competence and findings in patients with suspected community-acquired pneumonia in general practice.
citation: Strøm, J. J., Andersen, C. A., Jensen, M. B., Thomsen, J. L., Laursen, C. B., Skaarup, S. H., Schultz, H. H. L., & Hansen, M. P. (2025). Evaluating general practitioners' focused lung ultrasound competence and findings in patients with suspected community-acquired pneumonia in general practice. Scandinavian Journal of Primary Health Care, 43(2), 359-369. https://doi.org/10.1080/02813432.2024.2447083
title: Tailored three-component FLUS training program for general practitioners (theoretical self-study with validated MCQ test, one-day hands-on course with LUS-OSAUS assessment, and supervised real-life scans)
description: The training program prepared GPs to learn the indications for FLUS, execute the validated 14-zone FLUS protocol, and interpret findings. It "consisted of" theoretical self-study concluding with a validated multiple-choice test (pass cut-off score 20 of 0-30), a one-day hands-on course completing with a practical LUS-OSAUS assessment under standardised conditions, and five to ten FLUS scans in the GP's clinic supervised remotely by respiratory-medicine FLUS specialists at EFSUMB level III competence. Its content aligned with Danish and European Respiratory Society FLUS training courses.
requirements: Participants must pass the theoretical MCQ test at a cut-off score of 20 (range 0-30) and complete a practical LUS-OSAUS assessment, plus five to ten remotely supervised FLUS scans within one month of the hands-on course.
constraints: The study evaluated the program only in nine GPs who were already POCUS users, so generalizability to a broader GP population is uncertain.
target_learners: general practitioners using point-of-care ultrasound
target_learning_goals: learn indications for performing FLUS
execute the 14-zone FLUS protocol
interpret FLUS findings
examples: Nine GPs completed the program with MCQ-test scores between 20-26 (median = 25) and LUS-OSAUS scores of 96-100% of maximum (median = 99%).

Evaluating general practitioners' focused lung ultrasound competence and findings in patients with suspected community-acquired pneumonia in general practice. Scandinavian Journal of Primary Health Care, 43(2), 359-369. https://doi.org/10.1080/02813432.2024.2447083

article_title: Development and validation of a Chinese general practitioners' ability to recognise and manage depression assessment scale: a cross-sectional study.
citation: Zhang Yuqin, Sun Xuemei, Zhong Wen, Sun Dingkui, Gao Yingyan, Chen Xiyang, Zhang Weiru. (2025). Development and validation of a Chinese general practitioners' ability to recognise and manage depression assessment scale: a cross-sectional study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-094404
title: General Practitioners' Ability to Identify and Manage Depression assessment scale
description: A 24-item self-assessment scale with two dimensions, recognition (10 items) and management (14 items), measuring general practitioners' competence in recognising and managing depression in primary care. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale from 'completely unable' to 'completely able', and 'a total score is calculated, where a higher score reflects greater recognition and management capabilities'. The article describes it as 'straightforward' and resource-efficient compared with standardised-patient or psychiatrist re-evaluation methods.
requirements: Completed anonymously by GPs working primarily in community or primary care settings, based on their self-assessed ability to recognise and manage depression
constraints: The study did not include a direct comparison with other scales
Further validation in more diverse regions is needed to improve the scale's general applicability
target_learners: General practitioners in Chinese primary healthcare
target_learning_goals: Recognition of depression
Management of depression in primary care
examples: Administered online via Wenjuanxin questionnaires distributed through WeChat groups and academic forums between 2023 and 2024 across four development phases
key_sources: Zhang Yuqin, Sun Xuemei, Zhong Wen, Sun Dingkui, Gao Yingyan, Chen Xiyang, Zhang Weiru. (2025). Development and validation of a Chinese general practitioners' ability to recognise and manage depression assessment scale: a cross-sectional study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-094404

article_title: Developing a professional competency framework for general practitioners in tertiary hospitals in China: a modified Delphi study.
citation: Wei Yun, An Yanhua, Cao Qiumei, Feng Wei, Wang Dawei, Zhu Dan. (2025). Developing a professional competency framework for general practitioners in tertiary hospitals in China: a modified Delphi study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2023-082736
title: Professional competency framework for GPs in tertiary hospitals in China (4 primary, 12 secondary, 54 tertiary indicators)
description: A three-level professional competency framework for general practitioners in Chinese tertiary hospitals, developed via a modified Delphi process. It organises competency into four primary domains — medical services, teaching, research and prevention — with the final structure including "4 primary indicators, 12 secondary indicators and 54 tertiary indicators". It is intended for use in medical education, general practice research, quality improvement, GP self-evaluation and multisource feedback.
requirements: Consensus criteria: median score exceeding seven on a 9-point scale and at least 70% of panel ratings in the top tertile (7–9) for both importance and feasibility
constraints: The results may have limited generalisability due to expert selection
The effectiveness of the competency framework in real practice settings is unknown
target_learners: General practitioners in tertiary hospitals in China
GP residency trainees in tertiary hospital general practice departments
target_learning_goals: Professional competency assessment of GPs in tertiary hospitals
Competency feedback for GPs in China
examples: Two rounds of email Delphi surveys from August to October 2022 with 19 experts
Initial framework of 4 primary, 14 secondary and 48 tertiary indicators derived from a literature review of 31 published papers and three policy documents
key_sources: Wei Yun, An Yanhua, Cao Qiumei, Feng Wei, Wang Dawei, Zhu Dan. (2025). Developing a professional competency framework for general practitioners in tertiary hospitals in China: a modified Delphi study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2023-082736
